title: Never a Dixielander, and never finished learning
summary: He explains that pounding bass drums and press rolls swallowed the bass, and says no musician is ever complete.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: But you were saying that you didn't really identify with the Dixielanders ever.

No, I never did. And the reason being, when you played bass before the days of amplification, they had these giant bass drums, and the guys with big feet pounding on them -- and it's pretty difficult to really be heard. So that was one reason I didn't care for Dixieland music. The press rolls on the drums, they would swallow up all the bass notes. So I guess that's why I asked for $450, and I didn't get it. Well, I figured if I'm going to play this kind of music... You know, I'm still learning even in 1982, and I'm just beginning to be the kind of musician I hope to be some day.
You remind me of another musician I knew once, Mister Ellington, who used to call himself "an up-and-coming young bandleader," and that was in his seventies.

Well, I understand what he meant. Because you can play music... If I live to be 200... I've said this before. But you never can learn all there is to know. You only learn a little bit. So if you learn a little bit every day, you replenish a certain amount of knowledge. But there's no complete musicians. Some people might think they are, but they get carried away with themselves. You're never finished.
